title: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

content.overview: BNSS s. 356, Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender, is a procedural provision in the General provisions as to inquiries and trials cluster. Apply its conditions in sequence, identify the competent criminal court and remedy, and check the s. 531 transition rule before using BNSS or the saved CrPC.
content.glance: BNSS s. 356, Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender, is a procedural provision in the General provisions as to inquiries and trials cluster. Apply its conditions in sequence, identify the competent criminal court and remedy, and check the s. 531 transition rule before using BNSS or the saved CrPC.
content.study:
Current-law identity
BNSS s. 356 governs inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender within Chapter XXVI - General provisions as to inquiries and trials. The provision must be read with its enacted sub-sections, provisos, explanations, the BNSS First Schedule where classification or trial forum is relevant, and BNSS s. 355, BNSS s. 357.

Procedural meaning and legislative purpose
Criminal procedure is a sequence of safeguards, not a collection of isolated powers. This section allocates a procedural step to the police, Magistrate, trial court, Sessions Court or High Court and places conditions around its exercise. The mischief addressed is identified from the statutory text and Chapter setting; the court should not add a condition that the legislature did not enact or remove a safeguard that the text requires.

Mandatory application checklist
1. Identify the proceeding, procedural stage and order sought.
2. Confirm whether the investigation, inquiry, trial, application or appeal was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. If so, begin with BNSS s. 531(2)(a) and test whether the saved CrPC route governs.
3. Quote the exact operative words of s. 356, including every condition, proviso and explanation.
4. Identify the competent criminal court, territorial rule, statutory sanction or classification requirement.
5. Map each material fact to the statutory condition it proves or fails.
6. State the immediate remedy and the standard for interference.

Evidence and constitutional control
The procedural record remains subject to Articles 14, 20, 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The party asserting a factual foundation bears the ordinary burden under BSA s. 104; BSA s. 106 is limited to facts especially within a person's knowledge after the foundation is established. Electronic records must be separately tested under BSA s. 63 for the applicable certificate and production requirements. BSA admissibility does not cure an unlawful arrest, search, remand or other BNSS defect.

Courtroom method
In a written submission, state the current section first, identify the stage and forum, reproduce only the necessary statutory language, address the transition rule, apply each condition to the record, answer the principal objection, and request a precise order. Do not treat a police report as proof of guilt, an arrest as a conviction, a charge as a finding, or a procedural irregularity as automatically destroying the entire prosecution.

sections.heading: Provenance, Legislative Objective and Doctrinal Foundation
sections.body:
BNSS s. 356 regulates inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender within General provisions as to inquiries and trials.
Read the provision purposively but begin with its enacted text and the Chapter structure.
The constitutional background includes fair procedure, personal liberty and judicial accountability under Articles 14, 21 and 22.

sections.heading: Textual Anatomy, Provisos and Connected Provisions
sections.body:
Deconstruct every clause of BNSS s. 356; do not replace the provision with a CrPC summary.
Read it with BNSS s. 355, BNSS s. 357. A connected section may define the condition, forum, time limit or remedy without replacing this section.
Use historical concordance only to explain development, never as the current citation.

sections.heading: Mandatory Procedural Ingredients and Stage Test
sections.body:
First ingredient: the proceeding must be at the statutory stage addressed by s. 356.
Second ingredient: the competent officer or court must possess the relevant jurisdiction and power.
Third ingredient: each express condition, notice, reason, time limit, record or hearing requirement must be satisfied.
Fourth ingredient: the requested consequence must follow from the proved procedural breach or compliance; state the exact order sought.

sections.heading: BSA 2023 Burden and Electronic Evidence Checkpoints
sections.body:
BSA s. 104 supplies the ordinary burden framework; do not shift the initial burden merely by invoking s. 106.
BSA s. 106 applies to a fact especially within knowledge only after the party relying on the legal proposition establishes the necessary foundation.
Where electronic material is tendered, separately examine relevance, authenticity, integrity, source and BSA s. 63 certificate requirements.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Forum, Limitation and Transition
sections.body:
For proceedings under the post-1 July 2024 regime, cite BNSS s. 356 and verify the First Schedule or special statute where applicable.
For a matter pending immediately before commencement, apply BNSS s. 531(2)(a) and identify the saved CrPC procedure before addressing merits.
Check the applicable BNSS or special-statute limitation rule and calculate the remedy period from the actual order or event.

provisions.title: Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender

examples.title: Example 1 - Conditions satisfied
examples.body: A proceeding is at the stage governed by s. 356; the authorised officer or court records each statutory reason, follows the required notice and hearing path, and acts within jurisdiction. The order is tested against the section and its connected provisions.

examples.title: Example 2 - Boundary defect
examples.body: The decision-maker applies s. 356 without checking the procedural stage, the s. 531 savings rule or an express statutory condition. The advocate identifies the missing condition and seeks the precise procedural remedy rather than asserting an automatic result unsupported by the Act.

hypotheticals.question: Whether the order under BNSS s. 356 is sustainable and what immediate relief is available.
hypotheticals.analysis: 1. Identify the stage and whether the proceeding was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. 2. State the exact test in s. 356. 3. Verify jurisdiction, notice, reasons, time limits and hearing requirements. 4. Test the electronic record separately under BSA s. 63. 5. Grant only the remedy supported by the proved defect, such as modification, release, disclosure, remand correction, quashing where maintainable or appellate interference.

misconceptions.correction: Analyse BNSS procedure, BNS or special-statute liability, and BSA proof as separate legal layers.

cases.name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
cases.facts: The petitioner sought registration of information disclosing a cognizable offence.
cases.issue: Whether registration is mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Registration is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence, subject to the limited preliminary-inquiry framework recognised by the Constitution Bench.
cases.holding: The Court directed compliance with mandatory registration and confined preliminary inquiry to recognised categories.
cases.relevance: Use only where s. 356 concerns information, investigation or a connected pre-cognizance step; do not treat this case as authority for every BNSS provision.

cases.name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
cases.facts: The case concerned arrest and detention for an offence carrying imprisonment up to seven years.
cases.issue: Whether arrest and remand may be authorised mechanically in a lower-punishment case.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Police must satisfy and record the necessity conditions for arrest, and Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically.
cases.holding: The Court issued safeguards enforcing the discipline now reflected in the BNSS arrest framework.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 356 concerns arrest, custody, remand or liberty; otherwise identify a section-specific authority instead of forcing this case into the argument.

cases.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.facts: The Court addressed custodial violence and the absence of reliable arrest safeguards.
cases.issue: What minimum protections must accompany arrest and detention.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Arrest and custody require transparent documentation, accountability and safeguards protecting Articles 21 and 22.
cases.holding: The Court prescribed arrest and custody safeguards that inform the corresponding BNSS duties.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 356 directly engages arrest, custody, production or custody records; do not cite it as a substitute for the statutory text.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Provide a structured legal brief on BNSS s. 356 - Inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. ISSUE AND JURISDICTION
Identify the procedural stage, competent forum, commencement status and precise order sought.

II. RULE
BNSS s. 356 governs inquiry, trial or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offender. Read its clauses, provisos and connected provisions BNSS s. 355, BNSS s. 357; then test s. 531 savings.

III. APPLICATION
Map each fact to jurisdiction, statutory condition, notice, reason, time limit and evidentiary foundation. Test electronic records under BSA s. 63 and burdens under ss. 104-106.

IV. CONCLUSION
State whether the order stands, must be modified or requires a specific procedural remedy.

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
I. PROCEDURAL PROVENANCE
Set out the registration date, stage, orders and material relied upon.

II. STATUTORY SCHEME
Deconstruct BNSS s. 356, the Chapter setting, connected provisions BNSS s. 355, BNSS s. 357 and s. 531 savings.

III. MANDATORY INGREDIENTS
Address forum, jurisdiction, conditions precedent, notice, reasons, time limits, hearing and the statutory consequence.

IV. PRECEDENTS AND EVIDENCE
Use only verified authorities relevant to the proposition. Apply BSA ss. 63, 104-106 to digital and factual proof without shifting the initial burden improperly.

V. REBUTTAL AND PRAYER
Answer the transition, maintainability and merits objections, then seek the precise order supported by the record.

notes: Hardened student enhancement removing generic boilerplate.
Comprehensive analysis of the landmark new provision permitting inquiry, trial, and judgment in absentia of proclaimed offenders who have absconded.
Statutory text strictly follows Act No. 46 of 2023, s. 356.

learningObjectives: Master the statutory procedure governing inquiry, trial, or judgment in absentia of proclaimed offenders under Section 356 BNSS.
Understand the four cumulative pre-conditions under Section 356(1) required before commencing trial in absentia (warrant, proclamation, 90-day waiting period, and failure to appear).
Analyze mandatory fair trial safeguards: publication of notice in national newspapers, notification to relatives, and appointment of a State-funded defence advocate under s. 356(4).
Evaluate the legal effect of a judgment of conviction pronounced in absentia and the voluntary surrender/re-trial rules.
enhancement.definition: BNSS s. 356 establishes a groundbreaking procedure for conducting inquiry, trial, or pronouncing judgment in absentia of a proclaimed offender. When a person declared as a proclaimed offender under Section 84 has absconded to evade trial and there is no immediate prospect of arresting him, the Court may, after the lapse of ninety days from the date of the proclamation, proceed with the inquiry or trial, record evidence, and pronounce judgment of acquittal or conviction, provided mandatory statutory notices are published and a defence advocate is provided at State expense.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Expeditious justice, prevention of fugitive impunity, and procedural due process. Criminal proceedings cannot be held hostage indefinitely by fugitives fleeing the jurisdiction, provided rigorous procedural safeguards, constructive notice, and effective legal representation are guaranteed under Article 21.
statutoryFramework: Chapter XXVI — General Provisions as to Inquiries and Trials, BNSS s. 356.
Sub-section (1): Statutory threshold — person declared a proclaimed offender under s. 84, absconded to evade trial, no immediate prospect of arrest, and lapse of 90 days from proclamation.
Sub-section (2): Mandatory publication safeguards — notice published in two daily newspapers, served on last known address, and communicated to relatives.
Sub-section (3): Commencement of trial — court proceeds to record evidence of witnesses and try the charges.
Sub-section (4): Mandatory Legal Representation — appointment of an advocate to defend the accused at State expense.
Sub-section (7): Deposition validity — evidence recorded in absentia is substantive evidence binding on the accused upon future arrest.
essentialIngredients: The accused has been formally declared as a Proclaimed Offender under Section 84 BNSS.
The accused has absconded or is concealing himself to evade the trial, with no immediate prospect of arrest.
The expiration of an absolute statutory cooling-off period of ninety days from the date of issuance of the proclamation.
Issuance and publication of notice of trial in two local/national newspapers and communication to immediate relatives.
Mandatory appointment of a legal defence counsel at State expense to cross-examine witnesses and defend the case.
Recording of depositions of prosecution witnesses and formal pronouncement of judgment.
examples: Teaching illustration (Trial in Absentia of Economic Fugitive): Accused X commits bank fraud of ₹2,000 crores and flees to a foreign country with no extradition treaty. Non-bailable warrants are issued, followed by a Section 84 proclamation. Ninety days elapse without appearance. Notice is published in two prominent daily newspapers and served on his family. The Special Court appoints a senior legal aid advocate to represent X. The prosecution examines 40 witnesses, who are cross-examined by the defence counsel. The Court convicts X in absentia under Section 318 BNS and orders confiscation of his global assets.

Teaching illustration (Vitiation for Denying Legal Aid): In a trial in absentia under Section 356, the trial court proceeds to record prosecution evidence and convict the absent accused without appointing a defence advocate under Section 356(4). The judgment is unconstitutional and void: the provision of an advocate at State expense is an indispensable statutory and constitutional condition precedent.
distinctions: BNSS s. 356 vs CrPC 1973 s. 299: CrPC s. 299 only permitted recording evidence in the absence of an absconding accused for future use; BNSS s. 356 empowers the court to conduct a complete inquiry, trial, and pronounce a final judgment of conviction or acquittal in absentia.

Trial in Absentia vs Ex-Parte Civil Proceedings: Ex-parte civil decrees can be set aside upon showing good cause; a criminal judgment under Section 356 is a full judicial verdict rendered after testing evidence through a State-appointed defence advocate.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a Court of Session can commence trial in absentia under Section 356 BNSS against a proclaimed offender 45 days after the issuance of the proclamation under Section 84.
Rule: Under Section 356(1) BNSS, the court can proceed with the trial in absentia only after the lapse of an absolute statutory period of ninety days from the date of the proclamation.
Application: Only 45 days have elapsed; the statutory condition precedent of 90 days has not been fulfilled.
Conclusion: The commencement of the trial is premature, illegal, and contrary to Section 356(1) BNSS; the proceedings must be halted until the 90-day period expires.

shortAnswer: Define Section 356 BNSS as trial in absentia of a proclaimed offender.
State the four pre-conditions (proclaimed offender, absconding, 90 days elapsed, failure to appear).
Highlight the mandatory appointment of a defence advocate at State expense under s. 356(4).
tenMark: Introduction: Legislative rationale behind trial in absentia in countering fugitive impunity.
The procedural pathway: Section 84 proclamation followed by the 90-day waiting period.
Notice requirements: Publication in two daily newspapers and informing relatives.
Constitutional fair trial safeguards: Role of the State-appointed defence counsel.
sixteenMark: Constitutional jurisprudence: The right to be present at one’s trial under Article 21 versus the principle that no one can profit from their own wrong.
Exhaustive analysis of BNSS Section 356: Sub-sections (1) through (8).
Comparative study: Section 299 CrPC (preservation of evidence) versus Section 356 BNSS (full trial in absentia).
International perspectives: In absentia trials under French civil law, the Special Tribunal for Lebanon, and human rights benchmarks.
The mandatory defense counsel mechanism: Effective representation standards and testing prosecution witnesses.
Structured IRAC problem solving resolving a trial in absentia commenced prematurely.
Final synthesis on sovereign judicial authority under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita.

keyTakeaways: Section 356 BNSS enables full criminal inquiry, trial, and judgment in absentia of proclaimed offenders.
Can only be initiated after the lapse of 90 days from the proclamation under Section 84.
Mandates notice publication in two daily newspapers and notification to family members.
Mandatory appointment of a defence advocate at State expense is strictly required to preserve fair trial standards.
